title: Palm Trees: Technically, Giant Plants
summary: Josh and Chuck explore palm trees, opening with Chuck's origin story for the topic (a Los Angeles sales dinner) and then arguing that palms are giant plants, not trees, in botanical terms. They cover monocots versus dicots, primary versus secondary growth (and palms' "anomalous secondary growth"), the single apical meristem at the top, the fibrous adventitious root system, palm trunks and leaf scars, frond shapes (pinnate, palmate, costapalmate), palm flowers/inflorescences, monoecious and dioecious species, dates, coconuts and coconut water, palm wine, palm oil and its environmental issues, acai, hearts of palm, betel nuts, rattan and wicker, the double coconut palm, and how Florida's palms trace back to an 1878 shipwreck and Henry Flagler. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about Simpsons references.

segments.title: Opening banter and how the palm tree topic came about
segments.summary: Hosts promote live shows, then Chuck explains that the palm tree topic came from a Los Angeles sales dinner where he said topics come from looking around the world.

segments.title: Palms are not trees: giant plants
segments.summary: Josh introduces the key facts: there are more than twenty palm species, and botanists do not consider palms trees. Palm stems are described as stems, not trunks, and palms are closer to grasses than oaks.

segments.title: Angiosperms, monocots and dicots
segments.summary: Palms are angiosperms and monocots. Differences include seed leaves (cotyledons), leaf vein patterns, and the lack of a cambium layer and secondary growth in monocots.

segments.title: Primary versus secondary growth and palm girth
segments.summary: Dicot trees grow outward with annual rings through secondary growth. Palms grow upward, and their girth comes from vascular bundles increasing in size, which the hosts describe as anomalous secondary growth.

segments.title: Palm root systems and extreme palm species
segments.summary: Palms have adventitious roots without a central taproot, which makes them vulnerable to hurricanes. The hosts describe tiny palms, tall wax palms in the Andes, and the windmill palm in Atlanta.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Break before the palm content resumes; the hosts joke about the ad sales team.

segments.title: Palm fossils, Gondwana and palm trunk structure
segments.summary: Palm fossils are about seventy million years old, and palms may be older, spread by the breakup of Gondwana. The hosts cover palm trunk texture, leaf scars, and the optical illusion of bark-like scars.

segments.title: Apical meristem, spear leaves and crown shaft
segments.summary: New palm leaves emerge from a single apical meristem at the top of the plant, which is the only growing point apart from the roots. The spear, the crown shaft of king palms, and palm frond shedding are discussed.

segments.title: Frond shapes, palm flowers, and dioecious species
segments.summary: Pinnate, palmate and costapalmate leaves are described. Palm inflorescences are flowers, and species are monoecious or dioecious, which affects fruit production; dates are palm fruit.

segments.title: Coconuts, palm wine, palm oil, acai, hearts of palm and betel nuts
segments.summary: Coconut anatomy and coconut water versus coconut milk. Palm wine ferments quickly after tapping. Palm oil's environmental impact. Acai, hearts of palm, and betel nut chewing are covered. Rattan and wicker are discussed as palm products.

segments.title: Double coconut palm and Florida palm history
segments.summary: The double coconut palm has the largest seed. The 1878 Providencia shipwreck with about twenty thousand coconuts is said to have seeded Florida's coconut palms, with William Lane Heart and Henry Flagler also discussed. Flagler House Museum in Palm Beach is recommended.

segments.title: Listener mail: Simpsons references
segments.summary: A listener asks whether Josh skips Simpsons references on purpose; Josh says he occasionally holds back but not often.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts sign off with the show credit and a reminder to send email.
